content: Mouth sores can develop in various areas of the oral cavity, including the inner cheeks, gums, tongue, lips, or palate. These lesions can arise from a variety of causes, and their characteristics and underlying etiologies vary. Causes of Mouth Sores: 1. Cold Sores (Herpes Simplex Virus): Cold sores, also known as fever blisters, are caused by the herpes simplex virus (HSV). This virus is highly contagious. Before the sore appears, individuals often experience tenderness, tingling, or a burning sensation in the affected area. Cold sores typically begin as fluid-filled blisters that eventually crust over. The herpes virus remains dormant in the body and can reactivate due to triggers such as: Another illness, particularly one accompanied by fever. Hormonal fluctuations, such as those occurring during menstruation. Psychological or physical stress. 2. Canker Sores: Canker sores are not contagious and usually present as single pale or yellow ulcers with a red border, or as clusters of such lesions. The exact cause of canker sores is unclear, but potential contributing factors include: Viral infections. Temporary immune system suppression, such as during a cold or flu. Hormonal changes. Local irritation or trauma. Stress. Nutritional deficiencies, particularly low levels of vitamin B12 or folate. 3. Trauma or Irritation: Mouth sores can result from mechanical or thermal injury, such as: A sharp or broken tooth. Poorly fitting dentures. Biting the cheek, tongue, or lip. Burns from hot food or beverages. Braces or orthodontic appliances. Chewing tobacco. 4. Systemic Illnesses or Medications: Less commonly, mouth sores may indicate an underlying systemic condition, tumor, or adverse drug reaction. These include: Autoimmune diseases, such as systemic lupus erythematosus. Bleeding disorders. Malignancies. Infections, such as hand-foot-mouth disease. Immunosuppression, as seen in HIV/AIDS or post-transplant patients. Certain medications can also cause mouth sores, including: Aspirin. Barbiturates (used for insomnia). Chemotherapy agents. Gold compounds (used for rheumatoid arthritis). Penicillin. Phenytoin (used for seizures). Streptomycin. Sulfonamides. Risk Factors: Women are more prone to developing canker sores than men, possibly due to hormonal influences. When to Seek Medical Attention: Consult a healthcare provider if: A sore develops shortly after starting a new medication. Large white patches appear on the roof of the mouth or tongue, which may indicate thrush or another infection. A mouth sore persists for more than two weeks. You have a weakened immune system, such as from HIV or cancer. Accompanying symptoms include fever, skin rash, drooling, or difficulty swallowing. Treatment Options: Most mouth sores resolve spontaneously within 10 to 14 days, though some may persist for up to six weeks. Avoid hot, spicy, salty, or acidic foods and beverages. Gargle with cool water or consume popsicles, particularly for burns. Use over-the-counter pain relievers like acetaminophen. For canker sores: Rinse with salt water. Apply a paste made of baking soda and water. Use a mixture of equal parts hydrogen peroxide and water, applied with a cotton swab. Severe cases may require prescription treatments, such as: Fluocinonide gel (Lidex). Amlexanox paste (Aphthasol). Chlorhexidine gluconate (Peridex) mouthwash. Nonprescription products like Orabase can protect sores on the gums or inside the lips. Blistex or Campho-Phenique may alleviate discomfort from canker sores or fever blisters, especially when applied early. For cold sores: Ice application may provide relief. Antiviral medications may be prescribed for herpes-related sores. While some experts believe these drugs expedite healing, others argue they have minimal impact. Medical Evaluation: A physician will perform a thorough physical examination, focusing on the oral cavity, and may inquire about: The location of the sores (e.g., lips, gums, tongue, inner cheeks). Whether the sores are open ulcers. The presence of large white patches on the roof of the mouth or tongue. The duration of the sores (e.g., longer than two weeks). Previous occurrences of similar sores. Current medications. Associated symptoms, such as fever, sore throat, or halitosis. Treatment will depend on the underlying cause and may include: Topical anesthetics like lidocaine or xylocaine for pain relief (not recommended for children). Antifungal agents for oral thrush. Antiviral medications for herpes-related sores. Anti-inflammatory drugs for severe or persistent canker sores. Prevention: To reduce the risk of common mouth sores: Avoid consuming very hot foods or beverages. Manage stress through relaxation techniques, such as yoga or meditation. To minimize irritation: Chew food slowly. Use a soft-bristle toothbrush. Address dental issues, such as sharp teeth or ill-fitting dentures, promptly. For recurrent canker sores, consult a physician about supplementing with folate and vitamin B12. To prevent the spread of herpes sores: Avoid kissing or engaging in oral sex with someone who has an active cold sore. Refrain from these activities if you have an active sore. Do not share personal items like razors, lip balm, toothbrushes, or lipsticks. To prevent cancerous mouth sores: Avoid smoking or using tobacco products. Limit alcohol consumption to no more than two drinks per day.
